### What can be normalized—and what cannot

**A simple annualized comparison is only an estimate.** Dividing the disclosed three-year commitments by three gives Accenture approximately US$1 billion per year, PwC US approximately US$333 million per year and Capgemini approximately €667 million per year; these are arithmetic estimates from announced commitments, not realized annual spending. Deloitte’s “through FY2030” horizon does not provide a sufficiently precise comparable start-and-end period for the same calculation.

**The investment intensity judgment is therefore bounded.** Accenture and Deloitte have the strongest clearly disclosed global commitment anchors. EY has the strongest explicit reported EY.ai capability-build total among the Big Four, but its related amounts cover multiple scopes. Capgemini’s reported global commitment is large but secondary-reported. PwC’s amount is substantial but US-only, and KPMG’s primary amount is a US alliance practice. Bain has demonstrated equity-backed ecosystem commitment, while McKinsey, BCG and IBM emphasize platforms, partnerships, acquisitions or client delivery without one headline AI-investment number.

**The ranking condition is clear.** A defensible ranking would require AI-only realized spending for the same fiscal period, reporting entity, currency basis and treatment of acquisitions and alliances. Until those conditions exist, the strongest answer is a scope-qualified ledger rather than a league table.

### Commercialization is more visible than spending

**Accenture has the clearest commercial output set.** A 2026 secondary synthesis of Accenture’s FY25 disclosures reports US$5.9 billion in AI bookings, approximately US$2.7 billion in Gen/Agentic AI revenue and approximately 6,000 AI deployments, up from a handful in 2023. The metrics cover bookings, revenue and deployments—not the same economic measure—but together they show a visible conversion of investment into commercial flow. [6]

**IBM reports a larger but broader commercial construct.** IBM’s GenAI book of business exceeded US$12.5 billion since inception, but IBM defines that measure through revenue, SaaS contract value and consulting signings. It signals substantial market commercialization, not AI profit, realized investment or IBM Consulting-only revenue. [4]

**BCG reports client value rather than firm revenue.** BCG reports more than US$30 billion in value realized for clients from applied AI and more than 6,000 AI practitioners. This is a client-value claim, not BCG revenue, investment or audited cash return. BCG’s metric is strategically important because it shows the firm’s preferred value narrative, but it cannot be placed above or below Accenture’s revenue without a common denominator. [5]

**The other firms expose scale through different signals.** Deloitte reports more than 500 incubator projects and more than 1,000 pre-built agents. EY reports more than 100 Assurance capabilities or enhancements since 2022 and more than 30 new or enhanced capabilities in 2025. KPMG reports more than 55,000 Gemini Enterprise professionals, nearly 700 internally created no-code agents and dozens of go-to-market-ready agents. PwC reports internal platform adoption and client case metrics. Bain reports internal tool adoption and client productivity. Capgemini reports a quantified client vignette and survey results. These are meaningful outputs, but they are not interchangeable.

**The commercial mechanism is reusable intellectual property.** Firms invest in model access, data engineering, governance, delivery platforms, acquisitions and training. They then package that investment into assets that can be reused across clients: agent libraries, model-selection tools, workflow templates, sector accelerators, managed services and internal assistants.

**Client zero is a common accelerator.** EY’s internal Copilot deployment, IBM’s internal AI-first transformation, KPMG’s Gemini Enterprise adoption, PwC’s firm-wide upskilling and Bain’s Claude rollout all create environments in which the consultancy can test tools before selling implementation. This lowers delivery risk and creates demonstrations, but internal adoption is still an internal output, not proof of client value.

**Ecosystems extend delivery capacity.** The firms rarely build the entire model and infrastructure stack themselves. They combine their own industry methods, data, governance and change-management capabilities with Microsoft, Google Cloud, AWS, NVIDIA, OpenAI, Anthropic, IBM, SAP, Salesforce, Palantir and other partners. The commercial difference lies less in whether a firm has an alliance than in whether the alliance is connected to a reusable delivery platform and measurable production work.

**Managed services make AI recurring rather than episodic.** IBM’s Intelligent Operations, Accenture’s model managed services and SynOps, EY Managed Services, Capgemini’s WNS integration and Deloitte’s operations and audit platforms extend AI beyond a strategy project. The underlying mechanism is a shift from “recommend and hand over” to “design, deploy, operate and optimize,” which creates recurring service revenue but also increases responsibility for monitoring, security and performance.

## Big Four: Deloitte, PwC, EY and KPMG

### Deloitte

**Deloitte’s investment is global and implementation-oriented.** On 25 March 2025, Deloitte announced US$3 billion in global Generative AI investment through fiscal 2030 and expanded its Global AI Simulation Center of Excellence, first launched in Bengaluru. The center is intended to use simulations, digital twins and multi-agent systems to improve decision-making, risk management and return on investment. [2]

Deloitte also reports more than US$2 billion in global technology learning and development initiatives through the Deloitte Technology Academy. That amount is broader than AI and should remain separate from the US$3 billion GenAI commitment. [16]

**The operating model is regionalized experimentation followed by scale.** On 15 April 2024, Deloitte expanded its GenAI incubator network to eight hubs in the United States, Canada, India, Egypt, Malaysia, Poland, Portugal and Romania. The hubs give clients local environments to experiment, develop, deploy and scale GenAI solutions; Deloitte reported more than 500 client projects through the network. [17]

Deloitte’s 2026 agentic practice with Google Cloud extends that model into end-to-end transformation. Announced on 22 April 2026, the practice combines Google Cloud technologies including Gemini Enterprise with Deloitte Ascend and services spanning strategy, process redesign, implementation, governance and adoption. Priority industries are retail, health care, financial services and government and public services. [18]

**Deloitte’s products move from diagnosis to execution.**

|---|---|---|---|
| Enterprise AI Navigator, date not stated | Ascend-based advisory and implementation tool combining financial impact, workflow, process and technology readiness | Enterprise clients across industries | Client-specific transformation roadmap; performance metric undisclosed |
| Deloitte Ascend GenAI expansion, 2 Apr 2024 | Platform covering value cases, process design, program management, code, data conversion and testing | Enterprise applications and operations | Full delivery-lifecycle accelerators; client metric undisclosed |
| Global GenAI incubator network, 15 Apr 2024 | Regional experimentation-to-deployment hubs | Clients in 8 named markets | More than 500 client projects |
| Global AI Simulation Center, 25 Mar 2025 | Simulations, digital twins and multi-agent decision support | Power and utilities, monitoring, maintenance and hazard sensing | Scenario-based decision support; client KPI undisclosed |
| Enterprise Operating System with Palantir, 21 Jul 2025 | Deloitte IP and domain expertise combined with Palantir Foundry and AIP | Government and commercial ERP, finance, HR and supply chain | Federal case saved hundreds of thousands of person-hours |
| Google Cloud agentic practice, 22 Apr 2026 | Strategy, redesign, implementation, governance and adoption using Gemini Enterprise | Retail, health care, financial services and government | 1,000+ pre-built agents; more than 25,000 internal professionals; 100,000 licenses planned |
| Omnia connected agentic intelligence, 24 Jun 2026 | Network of agents coordinating audit and assurance workflows | Nearly 85,000 Deloitte Audit & Assurance practitioners worldwide | Global agent framework; productivity and quality metric undisclosed |

**The strongest named case is public-sector modernization.** On 21 July 2025, Deloitte said one of the largest federal agencies was using the Palantir-based Enterprise Operating System for ERP modernization and financial-management transformation. The implementation saved hundreds of thousands of person-hours while profiling years of complex data and process changes. The agency was not named and the exact hours were not reported. [19]

Deloitte also describes simulations for power and utilities involving real-time monitoring, preventive maintenance and hazard sensing. The output is a decision-support environment rather than a disclosed financial return. In April 2026, Deloitte and Google Cloud named Zebra Technologies as a client for intelligent operations, but the announcement provided no geography or KPI. [2][18]

**Governance is built into the delivery assets.** Deloitte’s Trustworthy AI posture emphasizes governance, controls, compliance, transparency and human oversight throughout the AI lifecycle. Omnia’s June 2026 announcement says its AI capabilities are aligned with the Trustworthy AI framework. Deloitte’s 2026 enterprise survey also reports that organizations where senior leadership shapes AI governance achieve greater business value than organizations that leave governance to technical teams alone. The survey establishes an association, not a causal effect. [20][21]

**Deloitte’s internal talent pipeline is unusually broad.** The AI Academy reports more than 120,000 professionals in training, 30-plus courses and thousands reaching the firm’s stated 100% AI-fluency standard. Deloitte also reports a trained and certified Forward Deployed Engineer cohort outside Palantir’s own organization and expects that cohort to more than triple within one year; the current cohort size is not stated. [22][19]

**The resulting judgment is implementation strength with a production caveat.** Deloitte has one of the clearest global structures for moving from local experimentation to sector-specific agents, governance and managed delivery. Its own 2026 survey supplies an important counterweight: only 25% of surveyed organizations had moved 40% or more of their AI pilots into production, while 54% expected to reach that threshold within three to six months. Deloitte’s model is therefore strongest where the buyer needs orchestration, industry controls and deployment capacity; the conclusion would change if the announced agent libraries and regional hubs failed to produce independently measured production outcomes. [23]

### PwC

**PwC’s investment is a US capability-and-alliance commitment.** On 26 April 2023, PwC US announced a planned US$1 billion investment over three years in AI capabilities, with Microsoft and Azure OpenAI at the center. The release said PwC had already begun implementing Azure OpenAI capabilities for clients in insurance, aviation and healthcare, but reported no named client or quantitative result. [10]

The same announcement targeted AI upskilling for 65,000 PwC US people under the My+ program. PwC later reported that more than 90% of its worldwide workforce were pursuing upskilling journeys, alongside apprenticeships and AI-and-human-skills immersion for new associates. [24]

**PwC’s strategic center is enterprise orchestration and work redesign.** Its 2026 predictions recommend a centralized AI studio combining reusable components, use-case assessment, a testing sandbox, deployment protocols and skilled people. The stated target functions include demand sensing, forecasting, hyper-personalization, product design, finance, HR, IT, tax and internal audit. PwC presents the technology-versus-work-redesign split as a rule of thumb: about 20% of value from technology and about 80% from redesigning work. That ratio is a recommendation, not a cross-client measurement. [25]

**The portfolio is increasingly productized.**

| Offering and date | Capability and delivery model | Customer or industry context | Output or performance signal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Azure OpenAI client implementations, 26 Apr 2023 | Implementation and advisory using GPT-4, ChatGPT and Azure OpenAI Service | Insurance, aviation and healthcare | Time and cost savings described qualitatively; metric undisclosed |
| ChatPwC, rollout date not stated | Private conversational AI using Azure OpenAI, Azure AI Document Intelligence and Azure AI Search; internal platform | Tax and global PwC professionals | Approximately 200,000 internal users in secondary synthesis |
| PwC One, item dated 17 Apr 2026 | Connected experience combining AI, data, agents and human expertise | Enterprise clients and PwC teams | Connected workflow and expert review; metric undisclosed |
| Eclipse, 2026 portfolio | Workflow and knowledge orchestration with prior insights and expert review | Enterprise advisory and delivery work | Workflow streamlining; metric undisclosed |
| Agent OS, 2026 recognition | Agentic workflow and enterprise operating capability | PwC US and enterprise clients | 2026 CIO 100 recognition; deployment volume undisclosed |
| AI studio model, 2026 forecast | Centralized components, assessment, sandbox and deployment protocols | Enterprise-wide programs | Recommended operating model; forecast, not measured deployment |

**PepsiCo demonstrates design output before financial output.** PwC and PepsiCo mapped more than 500 processes and data sources and designed 17 agentic-AI loops for an AI-native sustainability operating model. The case demonstrates process architecture, data mapping and agent design, but the public case excerpt does not provide savings, emissions, adoption or revenue metrics. [26]

**Customer operations provide the clearest quantified case.** PwC’s 2026 ROI study describes an unnamed major technology company with millions of customers. PwC designed an omnichannel contact center combining predictive intent modeling, adaptive dialogue, real-time analytics and an AI-agent management hub. The reported results were 25% less customer phone time, up to 60% fewer transfers, a seven-point increase in NPS and a ten-point increase in customer satisfaction. The client name and implementation date are not stated. [27]

**John Deere shows AI embedded in a physical workflow.** During the 2024 growing season, John Deere’s See & Spray used cameras and onboard computing to identify weeds and trigger nozzles selectively. PwC reports that the system covered more than 1 million acres, saved an estimated 8 million gallons of herbicide mix and produced 59% average herbicide savings across corn, soybean and cotton fields. The 8-million-gallon figure is explicitly an estimate, and the excerpt does not identify an independent evaluator. [27]

**Hiring and fan engagement extend the application range.** PwC reports that agentic AI helped Chipotle reduce time-to-fill by 75%, although the baseline and measurement period are not stated. PwC and the Seattle Mariners built Mariners Intelligence to unify fan data, personalize engagement and support ticket sales; the case listing reports no conversion or revenue metric. [28][29]

**Responsible AI is treated as an operating discipline.** PwC’s 2025 Responsible AI survey, cited in its 2026 predictions, reports that 60% of respondents associated responsible AI with improved ROI and efficiency and 55% with customer experience and innovation. Nearly half said operationalizing responsible-AI principles was difficult. PwC consequently emphasizes risk tiering, documentation, testing, monitoring, independent assurance and role-based upskilling. These are survey findings and recommendations rather than independently audited client results. [25]

**PwC’s evidence shows a value-concentration problem.** Its global CEO survey covered 4,454 CEOs across 95 countries and territories. Thirty percent reported increased AI-related revenue over the prior 12 months, 26% lower costs, 22% higher costs, 56% neither benefit and 12% both increased revenue and lower costs. PwC’s conclusion is that enterprise-wide deployment and work redesign distinguish the AI vanguard from broad experimentation. [30]

**The resulting judgment is workflow depth rather than platform breadth alone.** PwC’s distinctive proposition is to connect model access, business-process redesign, responsible AI and workforce adoption. It is a strong fit where the buyer’s problem is enterprise orchestration—finance, HR, tax, internal audit, customer operations and sustainability—rather than a standalone model deployment. The conclusion would change if PwC’s announced AI studio and Agent OS programs do not convert design artifacts and internal adoption into independently measured production outcomes.

### EY

**EY has the clearest reported EY.ai investment total among the Big Four.** EY launched EY.ai in September 2023 following US$1.4 billion in investment and reported a further US$300 million in FY24, for a stated total of US$1.7 billion in EY.ai investment. EY also reports a separate US$1 billion, four-year Assurance technology investment and a US$1 billion-plus, five-year EY–Microsoft initiative announced in 2026. [8][3][31]

**EY’s strategy is to make trust a data-and-platform property.** EY.ai combines EY business knowledge with AI embedded in EY Fabric and other proprietary technologies. Named components include the EY.ai Confidence Index for AI evaluation and monitoring, the EY.ai Maturity Model for benchmarking, the EY.ai Value Accelerator for prioritization, EYQ as a private large language model and the EY.ai Data Marketplace as a governed data foundation. The global EY organization operates in more than 150 countries, and EY Fabric is reported as serving 60,000 clients and more than 1.5 million unique client users. [8]

**The product portfolio combines platform, assurance and agentic layers.**

**Assurance is EY’s most developed AI product domain.** EY’s 2025 release introduced EYQ Assurance Knowledge, which searches and summarizes accounting and auditing content in context of engagement geography, industry and complexity. The capability is aligned with EY’s nine Responsible AI principles and its AI Assurance Framework, with users given access to vetted subject-matter sources and references. [31]

EY reports more than 30 new or enhanced Assurance capabilities in 2025 and more than 100 capabilities or enhancements since 2022. The output is substantial product development, but the release does not provide adoption, accuracy or client-financial metrics for each capability.

**EY’s client-zero evidence is unusually quantified.** In the May 2026 EY–Microsoft initiative, EY reported initially deploying Copilot to 150,000 users and recording a 15% productivity boost, which EY said it reinvested in client delivery and learning. EY is scaling Copilot across more than 400,000 people. Because the result is internal and company-reported, it demonstrates adoption and claimed productivity rather than independently measured client impact. [9]

**Finance, audit and tax provide concrete operating metrics.** EY reports that Microsoft Power Platform and Copilot Studio agents produced 95% faster finance lead times and a 37% or greater reduction in operational costs. The EY Canvas multi-agent framework covers 130,000 Assurance professionals across 160,000 engagements. Azure AI Document Intelligence on the Global Tax Platform reduced manual workload by up to 90%. All three are EY-reported internal results; the public release supplies no baselines, control groups or independent validation. [9]

**Singapore supplies a named client case.** Mercedes-Benz Singapore integrated EY.ai with Microsoft Azure OpenAI into software development for retail-sales applications. It reported an 80% auto-completion and accuracy rate for low-complexity code documentation and planned to extend AI into five additional software-development processes. The metric is client-reported and applies only to the stated documentation category. [32]

Keppel described an enterprise-wide AI and data transformation involving predictive maintenance, advanced analytics and GenAI across infrastructure, real estate and connectivity. Keppel’s stated targets were SGD 200 billion in funds under management and a 15% return on equity by 2030; these are corporate targets, not realized AI outcomes. [32]

**Talent development is both global and credentialed.** EY’s FY24 report says more than 250,000 people completed the AI Now course within its first six months, 40,000 AI badges had been awarded and another 40,000 were in progress. EY separately reports more than 100,000 AI, data and analytics credentials since 2018, and its AI and Data Challenge has attracted more than 45,000 participants across 146 countries. [3][33]

In Singapore, EY announced plans to upskill 500 Consulting professionals and develop an expected annual pool of 100 new joiners. The program targets finance, procurement, customer experience and HR capabilities. [32]

**The resulting judgment is trusted enterprise AI anchored in assurance.** EY differentiates itself through governed data, audit technology, responsible-AI principles, Microsoft engineering and NVIDIA infrastructure. Its evidence is strongest for internal platform adoption, assurance product output and finance/tax workflow metrics. The conclusion would change if the reported productivity and workload improvements were shown to have different baselines or if independent audits produced materially different results.

### KPMG

**KPMG’s investment record requires strict entity separation.** KPMG LLP’s 2024 announcement states a US$100 million investment in its Google Cloud practice and estimates US$1 billion in incremental growth. KPMG’s May 2023 global-member-firm announcement describes a firmwide generative-AI initiative but gives no amount. A secondary 2026 comparison cites a broader multibillion-dollar Microsoft cloud-and-AI commitment over five years; the figure and its exact scope are not public. [11][12][6]

**KPMG’s strategic identity is governed agentic implementation.** KPMG describes aIQ as a human-centric approach to becoming an AI-driven firm. Its Trusted AI posture emphasizes accountability, data integrity, explainability, transparency, sustainability, fairness, privacy, reliability, safety and security. KPMG’s alliance with Anthropic says AI should be engineered into platforms, controls and workflows where professional judgment matters. [34][35]

**The product portfolio connects trust controls to reusable agents.**

| Offering and date | Capability and delivery model | Customer or industry context | Output or performance signal |
|---|---|---|---|
| aIQ and Trusted AI, 4 May 2023 and ongoing | Human-centric AI operating approach with responsible-AI and security frameworks | KPMG workforce and clients | Nearly a dozen additional trainings identified in 2023; client metric undisclosed |
| Google Cloud Center of Excellence, Apr 2024 | Product development, industry expertise and technical resources aligned for GenAI delivery | Fortune 500 and global enterprises | Google Cloud practice bookings reported 10× higher over prior two years |
| Vertex AI Search and RAG agents, 2024 | Internal corpus search and grounded client agents across cloud providers | Knowledge assistance, data management, finance, health and retail | Development and internal deployment; client performance metric undisclosed |
| Agentspace and A2A collaboration, 9 Apr 2025 | Agent interoperability, Vertex AI Agent Builder and Agent Development Kit | Legal services, banking and other industries | Solutions under development; deployment metric undisclosed |
| KPMG Workbench, Jun 2025 | Multi-agent platform with Trusted AI assessment; underpins Clara, Digital Gateway and Velocity | Audit, tax and advisory workflows | Trusted AI stamp per asset in secondary synthesis |
| Gemini Enterprise firm adoption, 9 Oct 2025 | Agentic platform for internal adoption and client-zero learning | KPMG US and global client teams | Nearly 90% US employee access within two weeks; nearly 700 no-code agents |
| Agent Hero Program, 9 Oct 2025 | Hands-on client building and deployment of agents | Clients globally | Dozens of go-to-market-ready agents |
| Gemini finance solutions, 22 Apr 2026 | AI-native finance agents and forward-deployed engineering | Healthcare services and products, regulated sectors | Significant working capital described; amount undisclosed |

**KPMG uses internal deployment as a delivery laboratory.** On 9 October 2025, KPMG LLP reported that nearly 90% of employees accessed Gemini Enterprise within two weeks and that employees had created nearly 700 no-code agents since late September. The internal examples included proposal responses, configuration documents, tax planning content and client-facing audio briefings. These are internal adoption and asset-creation metrics rather than client financial outcomes. [36]

**The client programs focus on controlled enterprise workflows.** Finance agents target forecasting, anomaly detection, financial close and invoice processing. Procurement agents target contract leakage, automated sourcing and transaction insight. The Intelligent Modernization Toolkit applies GenAI to code conversion and testing. Workiva Sustainability implementations use Gemini Enterprise to connect data and support reporting for more than 85% of the Fortune 1000, although no individual client KPI is stated. [36]

**The 2026 healthcare case shows the regulated-workflow thesis.** KPMG reported using Gemini Enterprise for a major healthcare services and products company to automate pricing disputes, empower analysts and unlock significant working capital. The client and amount are undisclosed. The mechanism is clear: an agent handles a complex, manual finance workflow while analysts shift toward higher-value analysis and decision-making. [37]

KPMG’s AI Strategy material reports a manufacturer using AI to analyze tens of thousands of documents and achieve a 40% increase in research efficiency. It also describes an unnamed retailer with a 20% lighter employee workload and US$20 million in projected savings. The latter is explicitly projected, not realized. [38]

**Forward-deployed engineering closes the implementation gap.** In April 2026, KPMG said it was building a Forward Deployed Engineering capability with Google Cloud to put KPMG AI assets into real business environments. Engineers work with client teams to tailor solutions and accelerate implementation. The capability was being built at announcement; a realized aggregate impact metric was not reported. [37]

**The talent signal is access plus hands-on practice.** KPMG reports Gemini Enterprise deployment to more than 55,000 professionals globally in April 2026. Its 2023 release described nearly a dozen additional AI trainings, and the Google Cloud alliance included plans for more training and certifications. KPMG’s US adoption announcement gives stronger access data than completion data: access is not equivalent to certification or production capability. [37][12]

**The resulting judgment is governance-first practicality.** KPMG is strongest where AI must operate inside finance, procurement, legal, audit, tax, healthcare or public-sector controls. Its advantage is the combination of professional judgment, risk expertise, agent assets and hyperscaler implementation. The conclusion would change if the large internal adoption numbers did not translate into named production deployments with measured accuracy, savings and control outcomes.

## Accenture

### Investment, platformization and commercialization

**Accenture has the most complete disclosed scale story.** On 13 June 2023, Accenture announced US$3 billion over three years for its global Data & AI practice and a target of 80,000 AI professionals. The program covered hiring, acquisitions, training, data-and-AI readiness accelerators and pre-built industry and functional models across 19 industries. Accenture operates in more than 120 countries. [1]

A secondary synthesis of FY25 results reports approximately 77,000 AI and data professionals, 30,000 people trained through the NVIDIA Business Group, US$5.9 billion in AI bookings, approximately US$2.7 billion in Gen/Agentic AI revenue and approximately 6,000 AI deployments. ### McKinsey

**McKinsey’s investment scale is partnership- and capability-led.** The firm does not disclose a single firm-wide AI-investment amount in the examined evidence. Its principal current partnership anchor is the multiyear OpenAI Frontier alliance announced in February 2026, with financial terms undisclosed. QuantumBlack, AI by McKinsey, was acquired in 2015 and remains the principal specialist AI unit. [42][13]

**The Rewired method is the operating model.** McKinsey combines QuantumBlack and McKinsey Digital through six capabilities: a value-linked transformation roadmap, a skilled talent bench, a fast operating model, distributed flexible technology, embedded data and adoption and scaling. Its stated aim is to move organizations from AI experimentation to business- and operating-model redesign.

**Human judgment is McKinsey’s responsible-AI position.** The firm emphasizes multidisciplinary teams of strategists, technologists, data scientists, designers and engineers rather than autonomous AI replacing judgment. **The judgment is transformation depth rather than public investment scale.** McKinsey’s differentiator is the combination of industry strategy, operating-model redesign, technical talent and adoption. Its cases show measurable business outcomes, but the outcomes remain firm-reported. A stronger comparative conclusion would require a disclosed AI investment total and standardized production metrics.

### BCG

**BCG’s value proposition is people-and-process-led AI transformation.** BCG does not disclose a single firm-wide AI-investment amount in the examined evidence. It says the allocation is derived from thousands of consulting engagements. This is BCG’s own synthesis, not an independent cross-firm measurement.

BCG organizes services around three value plays:

- **Reshape:** redesign the enterprise.
- **Invent:** create new sources of growth.

BCG also reports a global consumer-health and hygiene company reducing manual-work time by 25%–40%, with up to 60% time savings in an insights-to-brief workflow. A PHOENIX group case describes improved service across 29 countries without a numeric cost or service metric. [5][44]

**The judgment is value capture, not investment leadership.** BCG is distinctive in explaining why technology alone does not produce enterprise value and in building sector products through BCG X. Its US$30 billion-plus figure should be read as reported client value, not BCG investment or revenue. The conclusion would change if independent evaluations found that the 10-20-70 allocation did not predict outcomes across clients or if the case metrics were redefined under common measurement standards.

### Why these application patterns recur

**Customer operations are the most accessible agentic entry point.** Customer-service workflows have high volumes, repeated intents, structured escalation paths and measurable outcomes such as handling time, transfers, satisfaction and sales. That explains PwC’s contact-center case, McKinsey’s Entel deployment and KPMG’s finance and procurement agents. Deloitte’s 2026 survey also identifies customer support as the area with the highest expected impact for agentic AI. [20]

**Finance and assurance reward controlled data.** Finance, tax and audit contain structured documents, rules, approvals and audit trails. EY’s Assurance Knowledge, KPMG’s pricing-dispute agent, Deloitte Omnia and IBM’s governed platform all exploit that structure. The trade-off is that accuracy, explainability, segregation of duties and human review matter more than raw generation speed.

**Software engineering is a bridge between copilots and agents.** Code documentation, testing, conversion and legacy-code modernization have clear artifacts and relatively fast feedback. Accenture’s switchboard, EY’s Mercedes-Benz case, KPMG’s Intelligent Modernization Toolkit, Bain’s legacy-code work and Capgemini’s FinTech case therefore show some of the earliest measurable results.

**Physical operations require data and process integration.** John Deere’s See & Spray, Rio Tinto’s scheduling platform and Deloitte’s power-and-utilities simulations demonstrate that AI value comes from connecting models to sensors, equipment, workflows and human decisions. The mechanism is not a chatbot; it is a closed or semi-closed sense, decide and act loop.

**Design artifacts precede financial returns.** PepsiCo’s process map and 17 agentic loops, Deloitte’s agent libraries, EY’s process flows and governance artifacts, and BCG’s sector products are outputs in their own right. They reduce uncertainty and create reusable architecture, but they should not be reported as cost savings or revenue unless a measured result exists.

### Output strength and evidence maturity

**Financial statements are the strongest evidence for corporate scale.** IBM’s annual report provides audited corporate revenue, R&D, acquisition spending and defined book-of-business measures. Those figures are more financially disciplined than a marketing case study, but they still do not isolate AI-only consulting investment.

**Client or partner cases are stronger when the client is named and the metric has a baseline.** John Deere’s acres and herbicide savings, Mercedes-Benz Singapore’s low-complexity documentation metric, EY’s internal finance figures and Avid Solutions’ error reduction have identifiable use cases. Even so, the sources are generally company- or client-reported rather than controlled studies.

**Internal adoption measures show readiness rather than value.** PwC’s internal user reach, KPMG’s 55,000 professionals, EY’s 150,000 Copilot users, Bain’s 7,000 Claude pilot users and Deloitte’s 25,000 Gemini users show deployment capacity. They do not establish external client performance.

**Forecasts should remain forecasts.** PwC’s 20%/80% work-redesign split, Deloitte’s expected production transition, Capgemini’s projected 2027 tailored-model share and Bain’s partnership plans describe direction or expectation. They become outcome evidence only after the relevant period and measurement are reported.

**Independent market analysis provides context, not complete validation.** Forrester’s May 2026 AI Consulting Services evaluation used provider profiles and customer feedback to compare firms including Deloitte, PwC, EY, KPMG, Accenture, IBM, BCG, McKinsey and Capgemini. It reports practice sizes, platform positioning and customer observations, but it does not independently audit every investment, case metric or client value claim. [43]

ISG’s October 2025 global GenAI-services report identifies a market transition from proof-of-concept experiments toward production deployments in customer service, document processing, software development and analytics. It also says robust multimodal deployments remain rare and that governance, integration, talent and ROI barriers can stall projects. [57]

A 2026 controlled field experiment involving 47 management consultants randomly assigned to no AI, general-purpose GenAI or specialized agent-based AI found that both AI-supported groups improved solution quality by 81%–104% and were up to 40% faster. Specialized agents did not robustly outperform the generic model, and the study was not firm-level or client-delivery evidence. [58]

| IBM | Hybrid-by-design AI, watsonx, agents and governed model choice | Private instances, guardrails, PII alerts and lifecycle governance | Mission-critical systems, finance, government, energy, HR and modernization | IBM, Red Hat, Microsoft, AWS, SAP, NVIDIA, Anthropic and others |
| Capgemini | Resonance, RAISE, WNS Intelligent Operations and five value pools | Trust by design, governance, data protection and reliable engineering | Supply chain, finance, HR, customer operations and sovereign cloud | Google Cloud, AWS, Microsoft, OpenAI, Mistral AI and SAP |

**The common direction is workflow embedding.** All ten firms are moving from chat interfaces and isolated pilots toward agents connected to enterprise data, applications, controls and operating processes. The practical implication is that a consulting buyer should evaluate data integration, process redesign, monitoring, human escalation and ownership—not only model quality.

**Deloitte and KPMG emphasize governed execution.** Their audit and risk heritage shapes platforms such as Omnia, Workbench, Trusted AI and forward-deployed engineering. This suits regulated sectors, but the model depends on turning governance controls into usable delivery routines rather than additional approval layers.

**PwC emphasizes work redesign.** Its AI-studio recommendation and 20%/80% value rule place operating-model change above software acquisition. This increases the importance of leadership, role redesign and workforce trust, but it also makes results more dependent on client organizational change.

**EY emphasizes assurance-grade foundations.** EY combines governed data, Assurance technology, Microsoft engineering, NVIDIA infrastructure and client-zero internal deployments. The implication is a stronger proposition for finance, tax, audit, risk and regulated use cases where traceability and confidence matter.

**Accenture emphasizes industrialization.** Its combination of platforms, acquisitions, managed services, model customization and commercial metrics suggests the most vertically integrated route from strategy to operating AI. That scale can accelerate delivery but may make the buyer more dependent on Accenture’s ecosystem and proprietary assets.

**McKinsey and BCG emphasize transformation logic.** McKinsey’s Rewired model and BCG’s 10-20-70 model explain why adoption, process change and human capability determine value. Their strategic advantage is diagnosis and redesign; their risk is that the boundary between method, advisory and measurable delivery remains less visible than in a product-led platform.

**Bain emphasizes partner-enabled deployment.** OpenAI and Anthropic relationships give Bain access to frontier models and enterprise deployment resources. Its differentiation is co-design and production enablement rather than ownership of a single platform.

**IBM emphasizes control over the enterprise stack.** Hybrid cloud, watsonx, infrastructure, data, consulting and managed operations allow IBM to connect AI to mission-critical environments. The implication is strong fit for organizations where sovereignty, security, integration and long-lived systems outweigh rapid experimentation.

**Capgemini emphasizes operations and sovereignty.** The WNS acquisition, Resonance framework, RAISE platform and sovereign-cloud partnerships position Capgemini around agentic operations at scale. The opportunity is broad process transformation; the risk is integration complexity after a large acquisition and the need to convert survey-led market momentum into audited client results.

**Deloitte and Capgemini emphasize breadth.** Deloitte’s Academy reaches more than 120,000 professionals, while Capgemini reports hundreds of thousands trained in GenAI and Agentic AI. Their opportunity is widespread fluency; their execution risk is that broad access may not create enough specialist talent for architecture, evaluation, security and agent operations.

**Accenture and BCG emphasize specialist capacity.** Accenture combines a large AI-and-data workforce with NVIDIA training, Stanford certification and acquisitions. BCG combines practitioners with BCG X engineers, data scientists, designers and product managers. Their operating advantage is deeper build capability; their measurement challenge is defining who counts as an AI specialist.

**EY and KPMG link learning to governed internal deployment.** EY’s AI Now, badges, Copilot deployment and Assurance platform create a connection between learning and daily workflows. KPMG’s Gemini Enterprise adoption and no-code agent creation create a similar feedback loop. In both cases, access and use are stronger evidence than completion or post-training productivity.

**IBM and PwC have the largest explicit access ambitions.** IBM’s 2-million-learner target is external and global, while PwC’s 65,000-person target is PwC US and its later 90%-plus participation figure is worldwide. Neither measure is equivalent to the number of production-capable consultants.

**The future execution question is role transition.** Deloitte identifies insufficient worker skills as the biggest barrier to integrating AI into workflows. Accenture reports that only 5% of organizations were reskilling at scale despite 94% of workers saying they were ready to learn new GenAI skills. Capgemini’s survey expects 63% of employees to experience a role transition by 2027–2028. These figures are survey-based forecasts, but they point to the same constraint: talent development must change job design, governance and incentives, not only teach prompt use.

| Reader need | Firms and offerings to inspect first | Evidence to examine | Selection question |
|---|---|---|---|

**The buyer should compare evidence maturity before comparing percentages.** A named client with a baseline and a production date is stronger than an unnamed case with a large percentage. A measured internal productivity result is stronger than a forecast, but weaker than an independently designed client study. A financial filing is strongest for corporate scale, but it may say little about a specific consulting implementation.

The firms’ disclosed output categories can be read as a sequence:

1. **Capability formation:** investments, acquisitions, partnerships and training.
2. **Reusable assets:** platforms, methods, agents, model catalogs and process libraries.
3. **Internal deployment:** client-zero use, workforce access and tool adoption.
4. **Client implementation:** pilots, proofs of concept and production workflows.
5. **Measured outcome:** time, cost, quality, revenue, productivity or customer metrics.
6. **Independent validation:** external evaluation, controlled studies or assurance.

Most firms have reached the second and third stages across a broad portfolio. Accenture, IBM and selected Big Four practices disclose more commercial and internal deployment evidence. Named client outcomes are increasing, but independent validation remains concentrated at market level rather than individual-firm case level.

The figures use different definitions, units, currencies, reporting entities and measurement bases. Investment amounts may be announced commitments, reported capability build, alliance or practice spending, acquisitions, equity stakes or broader R&D; bookings, revenue, book of business and client value are separate constructs. Workforce figures may count learners, users, credentials, practitioners, technical staff or training participants. Many case metrics are firm- or client-reported, some clients are unnamed, several results are projected or survey-based, and announcements, pilots, internal deployments, production implementations and independently evaluated outcomes are not equivalent. Capgemini Research Institute statistics describe surveyed organizations rather than Capgemini spending or audited client returns, and McKinsey, BCG and IBM do not disclose one comparable firm-wide AI-investment total in the examined evidence. The comparison is current through 13 September 2026; a like-for-like ranking would require common periods, scopes, realized AI-only spending, standardized production definitions and independent outcome measurement.

## Closing judgment

The global consulting market has moved beyond selling AI as a presentation topic. The leading firms now sell combinations of models, data foundations, agents, governance, operating-model redesign, implementation and managed operations.

Accenture is the clearest scale-and-commercialization benchmark. Deloitte, EY and KPMG are strongest where trust, assurance and regulated workflows dominate. PwC is distinctive in linking enterprise AI to work redesign. McKinsey and BCG remain strategy-plus-build firms whose principal contribution is transformation architecture and value capture. Bain is using frontier-model partnerships to accelerate deployment. IBM combines AI products, infrastructure and consulting at unusual depth. Capgemini is building an agentic-operations and sovereign-ecosystem position.

The practical conclusion is not that one firm leads every category. It is that the choice should follow the client’s bottleneck: platform industrialization, regulated control, operating-model change, sector-specific production, hybrid-cloud integration, workforce transformation or business-process operations. The firms’ investment announcements create capacity; their reusable assets create commercialization; their client deployments create evidence; and their talent and governance programs determine whether that evidence becomes durable enterprise value.
